source_refs.note: Physical properties of alkenes (printed as a second 11.6.2) with Quick Check 11.4, page 256.

items: First three members i.e. ethene, propene and butene are gases at room temperature while C₅ to C₁₅ are liquids and the higher members are solids.
They are insoluble in water but soluble in alcohol.
They have characteristic smell and burn with luminous flame.
Unlike alkanes, they show weakly polar properties because of sp² hybridization

blocks.prompt: a) Give the reactions of propanol with H₂SO₄, write down all the reaction involved.
blocks.explanation:
With concentrated sulphuric acid, propan-1-ol first forms propyl hydrogen sulphate:
CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + H₂SO₄ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OSO₃H + H₂O
On heating this decomposes to propene:
CH₃CH₂CH₂OSO₃H → CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂SO₄
Overall the alcohol is dehydrated.

blocks.prompt:
b) Name the following alkenes:
i) CH₃C(CH₃)=CH-CH₃
ii) CH₂=CHCH(CH₃)₂
blocks.explanation:
i) CH₃C(CH₃)=CHCH₃: a four-carbon chain with the double bond at C2 and a methyl group at C2: 2-methylbut-2-ene.
ii) CH₂=CHCH(CH₃)₂: a four-carbon chain with the double bond at C1 and a methyl group at C3: 3-methylbut-1-ene.

blocks.prompt:
c) Draw the structural formulas of the following alkenes.
i) 3-Methyl-2-butene
ii) 2-Methyl-4-ethyl-2-pentene
blocks.explanation:
i) 3-Methyl-2-butene (3-methylbut-2-ene) is CH₃CH=C(CH₃)CH₃. Numbered correctly (the double bond gets the lower number), it is the same molecule as 2-methylbut-2-ene.
ii) 2-Methyl-4-ethyl-2-pentene is CH₃C(CH₃)=CH–CH(CH₂CH₃)–CH₃: a five-carbon chain with the double bond at C2, a methyl group at C2 and an ethyl group at C4. The longest chain runs through the ethyl group and has six carbons, so the correct name of this molecule is 2,4-dimethylhex-2-ene.

blocks.prompt: d) Give the dehydrohalogenation reaction of bromopropane?
blocks.explanation:
1-Bromopropane loses HBr when heated with alcoholic KOH:
CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + KOH(alcoholic) → CH₃CH=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O

blocks.prompt: e) Can propanol undergo dehydration? If yes give reactions involving dehydration.
blocks.explanation:
Yes. Heated with concentrated sulphuric acid, propan-1-ol loses a water molecule and gives propene, through propyl hydrogen sulphate:
CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + H₂SO₄ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OSO₃H + H₂O
CH₃CH₂CH₂OSO₃H → CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂SO₄
